Toronto Blessing
tuh-RON-toh BLES-ing
movement
From Toronto (the city of its origin) and blessing; a charismatic revival movement of the mid-1990s.

Biblical Definition

The Toronto Blessing was a charismatic revival movement that began in the mid-1990s at a church near the Toronto airport and spread widely, marked by extraordinary physical phenomena attributed to the Holy Spirit—uncontrollable laughter, falling to the ground, shaking, weeping, and even animal sounds such as roaring and barking. Its defenders hailed these manifestations as a fresh outpouring of the Spirit; its critics, including many within the broader charismatic world, judged them to be disorderly and without scriptural warrant. Measured by the Word, the movement illustrates the danger of seeking and validating spiritual experience apart from the test of Scripture. The Bible nowhere presents such uncontrolled phenomena as marks of the Spirit’s work; on the contrary, the Spirit is the author not of confusion but of peace, the fruit of the Spirit includes self-control and temperance, and all things in the assembly are to be done decently and in order. The true and abiding works of the Spirit are conviction of sin, the exaltation of Christ, the love of the truth, growth in holiness, and the fruit of love, joy, peace, and the rest—none of which is measured by physical sensation or ecstatic display. The dictionary names the Toronto Blessing as a cautionary instance of experience-driven religion divorced from the Word: spiritual phenomena, however intense, are not self-authenticating, and every spirit must be tried whether it be of God. The Spirit’s genuine work always honors Christ, accords with Scripture, and bears the orderly fruit of holiness, not the spectacle of the flesh.

Webster 1828 Definition

A mid-1990s charismatic revival marked by uncontrolled laughter, falling, shaking, and animal sounds—a cautionary case of experience-driven religion divorced from the Word and the Spirit’s orderly fruit.

TORONTO BLESSING, a charismatic revival movement of the mid-1990s.

Began at a church near the Toronto airport and spread widely.

Marked by uncontrolled laughter, falling, shaking, weeping, and animal sounds.

Hailed by defenders as an outpouring of the Spirit; judged by critics as disorderly.

A cautionary case of seeking spiritual experience apart from the test of Scripture.

Key Scripture

1Co 14:33 — "For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints."

1Co 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Gal 5:22 — "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,"

1Jo 4:1 — "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."

Modern Corruption

Spiritual experience is sought and validated apart from Scripture, mistaking uncontrolled phenomena for the Spirit’s work.

expand to see more

The corruption is the validating of spiritual experience apart from the test of the Word. The uncontrolled laughter, falling, shaking, and animal noises of the movement were taken as self-evident marks of the Spirit, though Scripture nowhere presents such phenomena as His work. But the Spirit is the author not of confusion but of peace; His fruit includes temperance and self-control; and all things in the assembly are to be done decently and in order. Phenomena that overthrow self-control and decorum bear the marks of the flesh or worse, not of the Spirit of order.

The dictionary names the Toronto Blessing as a cautionary instance of experience-driven religion, while distinguishing it from the genuine, abiding works of the Spirit. The true marks of the Spirit’s presence are conviction of sin, the exaltation of Christ, love of the truth, growth in holiness, and the orderly fruit of love, joy, and peace—none measured by physical sensation. John commands that the spirits be tried whether they are of God; intensity of feeling is no proof of divine origin. The remedy is not to quench the Spirit but to test every claimed manifestation by the Word, which honors Christ and produces holiness, not spectacle.

Hebrew Roots

The movement’s name marks its origin and its claim; the dictionary tests its phenomena by the Spirit’s orderly fruit.

expand to see more

“Toronto” — the city near whose airport the movement began.

“Blessing” — the movement’s claim to a fresh outpouring of the Spirit.

Tested by “decently and in order” and the fruit of self-control.

“Try the spirits whether they are of God” — the rule for all such claims.

Allied with later experience-driven charismatic movements.

Usage

"The Toronto Blessing is cited as a case of experience divorced from the Word."

"Its phenomena are tested by the Spirit’s fruit of order and self-control."

"It illustrates the duty to try the spirits rather than trust intensity of feeling."
